chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Taxonomy of Alternative Data

lessons.title: Text and Sentiment Data: News, Social Media, and Regulatory Filings

body.text: Text is data too, but only after you accept that a word means something different in an annual report than it does in a movie review.

children.text: Text and sentiment data turns unstructured writing, filings, news, transcripts, social posts, into a structured, numeric signal. It is the widest category in this course, spanning sources that decay in minutes and sources that take real analytical effort to even read correctly. This lesson covers four of them, why standard sentiment tools misread financial language, and where India's language mix and social media landscape create problems most global NLP tools were never built for.
Four Text Sources on the Speed vs Depth Spectrum

body.caption: The faster a text source decays, the less analysis it usually requires to extract

cells: Official disclosures filed with NSE and BSE: board outcomes, credit rating actions, related party transactions
Minutes to hours, since it is public disclosure by design and every desk can scrape it the instant it posts
Real-time news headlines and articles scored for tone and event type
Hours to a day, faster for sudden shocks, slower for gradually building narratives
Retail chatter across platforms, often around results, rumours, or price moves
Very fast, often intraday, but extremely noisy and prone to manipulation
Management commentary and the Q&A exchange with analysts
Weeks to quarters, since extracting tone and hedging cues properly takes real linguistic modelling, not a quick keyword count

children.text: Why General-Purpose Sentiment Dictionaries Fail on Financial Text

markDefs.definition: A widely used finance-specific set of word lists, built by researchers Tim Loughran and Bill McDonald, developed after they found that general-purpose sentiment dictionaries badly misclassify ordinary financial and legal vocabulary.

children.text: A sentiment dictionary built for movie reviews or product feedback will flag routine financial vocabulary as negative simply because those words carry a negative connotation in everyday English. This is the exact problem researchers Tim Loughran and Bill McDonald documented and fixed with their

, now a standard reference in financial text analysis published in their well known Journal of Finance study on textual analysis of company filings. If your NLP pipeline still uses an off-the-shelf, general-purpose sentiment model on Indian annual reports or earnings call transcripts, it is very likely scoring routine disclosure language as bad news.

columns.label: Generic Sentiment Dictionary
points: 'Tax' scored as negative, because taxation feels burdensome in everyday usage
'Liability' scored as negative, carrying its common blame-related meaning
'Cost' and 'depreciation' scored as negative, sounding like loss or decline
Built from movie reviews, product feedback, or general news text

columns.label: Finance-Specific Dictionary
points: 'Tax', 'liability', 'cost', and 'depreciation' scored as neutral, since they are routine accounting terms in a filing
Negative words are reserved for terms like 'default', 'litigation', 'restatement', and 'impairment'
Uncertainty words like 'may', 'could', and 'approximately' are tracked as their own separate category, not folded into positive or negative
Built specifically from analysis of company filings and financial disclosure language

body.title: Spot the Miscategorized Word
body.question: Which of these words is most likely to be wrongly flagged as strongly negative by a generic, off-the-shelf sentiment dictionary applied to an Indian company's annual report, even though it is routine and neutral in that context?
body.explanation: Depreciation is a completely routine, mandatory accounting term appearing in nearly every set of financial statements, and it carries no negative implication about the business in that context. A generic dictionary, however, sees a word that sounds like decline or loss in everyday English and often scores it negative. Default, litigation, and restatement are genuinely negative signals even in a finance-specific dictionary, so both types of dictionary would correctly flag them.

children.text: Racing the Clock: Parsing Exchange Announcements the Moment They Post

Because filing text decays in minutes, the engineering challenge is not clever NLP, it is speed and reliable classification. A typical pipeline polls the exchange's public announcement feed at short intervals, deduplicates new filings against what it has already seen, extracts the text from HTML or PDF, and classifies the announcement type, board outcome, rating action, related party transaction, before deciding whether it is even relevant to your watchlist.

body.caption: A skeleton for a filing-monitoring loop: poll, dedupe, classify, alert. The actual data connection must come from a licensed or officially sanctioned feed, not an ad hoc scrape of a page you have not checked the terms of service for.

children.text: Earnings Call Tone: Reading What Management Doesn't Say

Earnings call transcripts reward slower, deeper analysis. Beyond simple positive or negative scoring, researchers track hedging and uncertainty language: a rising frequency of words like 'we believe', 'to the best of our knowledge', 'may', and 'could', vague non-answers to specific analyst questions about margins or receivables, and a sudden drop in specific numeric guidance compared to prior quarters. None of these are proof of a problem on their own, but a consistent rise in hedging language, especially concentrated around a specific topic an analyst keeps pressing on, is a pattern worth flagging for closer fundamental review.

body.title: Two Answers to the Same Analyst Question
body.scenario: An analyst on an earnings call asks two different companies the same question: 'Can you walk us through the increase in receivable days this quarter?' Company A's CFO responds: 'Receivable days rose from 45 to 52 due to a large order from a state utility customer with a longer payment cycle, which we expect to normalize by Q3 as that invoice is collected.' Company B's CFO responds: 'We believe our overall collections process remains broadly satisfactory, and we are confident that, to the best of our knowledge, working capital dynamics will likely improve going forward.'
body.prompt: Which response should raise more concern for a text-based hedging analysis, and why, independent of whether either company's numbers are actually fine?
body.modelAnswer: Company B's response should raise more concern from a pure text analysis standpoint. It never answers the specific question asked, gives no number, no named cause, and no concrete timeline, while stacking hedging phrases such as 'we believe', 'to the best of our knowledge', and 'likely' around a vague, generic reassurance. Company A's response, even though receivable days actually got worse, is specific: it names a cause, quantifies the change, and gives a concrete expectation for when it resolves. A hedging-language model should score Company B's answer as higher risk than Company A's, because vagueness and evasiveness under direct questioning is the pattern this technique is built to catch, not the mere fact that a metric moved in an unfavourable direction.

children.text: Social Media and the Hinglish Problem

Retail sentiment on social platforms can move fast around results and rumours, but Indian retail chatter is often written in Hinglish, English and Hindi mixed within the same sentence, or in regional languages, which most off-the-shelf English sentiment models handle poorly. A model trained purely on English financial text will silently under-read a large share of genuine Indian retail sentiment rather than fail loudly, which is a more dangerous kind of error because it looks like the model is working. There is also a regulatory dimension worth knowing: SEBI has issued advisories and taken action around unregistered 'finfluencers' giving investment advice on social platforms, a reminder that some of the loudest voices generating this text may themselves be operating outside SEBI's investment adviser framework, which is a reason for extra scepticism, not extra weight, when a single influential post drives a sentiment spike.

body.title: Manipulation risk: not every sentiment spike is organic

children.text: Social sentiment is uniquely exposed to coordinated manipulation, groups of accounts posting in a short window to simulate organic enthusiasm ahead of a pump, or coordinated negative posts to trigger a sell-off. Robust use of this data means checking for account diversity, posting time clustering, and unusually templated language before treating a spike as genuine demand or genuine concern, and treating social sentiment as one noisy input to combine with other sources rather than a standalone strategy.

body.text: The fastest text source is also the least trustworthy on its own, and the most trustworthy text source is also the slowest to extract. Filing feeds, news, social chatter, and earnings call tone are not competing for the same job, they answer different questions at different speeds.

The earnings call exchange in this lesson is a constructed hypothetical for teaching purposes, not a transcript of any real company or executive. Nothing here is a recommendation to trade any security. Always confirm you are operating within a data feed's terms of service and applicable law before building any scraping or monitoring pipeline.

points: Text data spans four sources with very different speed and depth trade-offs: exchange filings (fastest, shallowest), news wires, social media (fast, noisy), and earnings call transcripts (slowest, deepest)

General-purpose sentiment dictionaries misclassify routine financial vocabulary like tax, liability, cost, and depreciation as negative, which is exactly why finance-specific word lists like Loughran and McDonald's exist
Filing-monitoring pipelines win on speed and reliable classification, not on sophisticated language modelling, since the text itself is short and structured
Earnings call hedging analysis looks for vague answers, rising uncertainty language, and evasiveness under specific questioning, not just whether a metric moved in a good or bad direction
India's Hinglish and regional-language retail chatter is poorly handled by English-only sentiment models, creating a silent under-reading problem rather than an obvious failure
SEBI's scrutiny of unregistered finfluencers is a reason for extra scepticism, not extra confidence, when a single social media post appears to be driving a sentiment spike
Social sentiment is uniquely exposed to coordinated manipulation and should be checked for account diversity and posting patterns before being trusted as an organic signal
